title: Frightening children
translation: Yan Hui, Confucius's best student, wanted never to put a burden on anyone. Don't make people suffer, and don't treat anything cruelly. Even the poorest man has a will of his own, and you have no right to take it from him.

Some people think it's fun to trick little children, scare them, or tease them until they're ashamed. Grown-ups think it's nothing, since none of it is real. But a small child feels the fear, the shame and the shock right through. Tormenting a child for fun is not kind.

And grown-ups are no different. Our joy and anger, our grief and pleasure are all illusions too, but who doesn't take them for real? Hurting someone's mind does them more harm than hurting their body.

Most illness comes from the mind, too. Very little comes from outside. Sometimes you take medicine to make you sweat and nothing happens, but the moment you feel ashamed or scared, you sweat every time. That's the mind at work. In China, a man was once sent high up a tower to write its name board, and he came down with white hair.

literal: Yan Hui's aim was not to impose toil on others.
In general, making people suffer and treating things cruelly: one must not take away even the will of a lowly commoner.
Also, there are those who deceive and frighten small children, shame them with words, and amuse themselves.
Grown-up people think it is nothing because it is not real, but to a child's heart the feeling, frightening, shameful and dismaying, sinking into the body, must be truly intense.
To torment them and be amused is not a heart of compassion.
The joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure of grown-up people too are all illusion, but who does not cling to them as having real existence?
Rather than injuring the body, causing pain to the heart harms a person even more.
As for contracting illness, too, most of it is contracted from the heart.
Illnesses that come from outside are few.
When one takes medicine and seeks to sweat, there are times it has no effect, but once one feels shame or fear, one always sweats: one should know that this is the work of the heart.
It is not without precedent that someone wrote the plaque of the Lingyun (tower) and became a white-haired man.

notes.quote: 顔回は、志人に労を施さじとなり
notes.text: Yan Hui, Confucius's favourite student. In the Analects, asked what he wishes for, he says he would like not to boast of his good points and 無施勞, which can be read 'not to make a show of my efforts' or, as Kenkō takes it here, 'not to put burdens on others'. The 'not boasting' half comes back in section 130.

notes.quote: 賎しき民の志をも奪ふべからず
notes.text: An echo of another line in the Analects: an army can be robbed of its commander, but an ordinary man cannot be robbed of his will.
{虐|しへた}ぐ: 'to treat cruelly, to oppress' (modern {虐|しいた}げる). The reading is the 1925 edition's. {物|もの} here covers living things, not only people.
{賺|すか}す: 'to trick, to coax'. {嚇|おど}す: 'to frighten'. Both readings are the 1925 edition's.
おとなし: 'grown-up, mature', the same false friend as in section 236. Not modern 'quiet, well-behaved'.

notes.quote: 誰か実有の相に著せざる
notes.text: Buddhist terms. {虚妄|こまう}: 'illusion, empty'. {実有|じつう}の{相|さう}: 'the appearance of really existing'. {著|ぢやく}す: 'to cling to', as in {執著|しふぢやく}, attachment. か … ざる: a rhetorical question, 'who does not cling? (Everyone does.)' So grown-ups, too, are hurt by things that are not real.
{験|しるし}: 'effect'. Making a patient sweat was a standard treatment, and the medicine did not always work.

A Chinese story about the calligrapher Wei Dan (third century), told in the Shishuo Xinyu and retold in Japanese collections: he was hauled high up to write the name board of a tower, and when he came down, his hair had turned white. Versions differ on the building's name; 凌雲 means 'above the clouds'. {例|ためし}なきにあらず: 'it is not without precedent'.
